title: Achillis mors
titleEn: The Death of Achilles — Metamorphoses XII.580–628
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Neptune, grieving for a son turned into a bird and hating Achilles as the ravager of the walls he and Apollo built to no purpose, asks Apollo to shoot him down from cover; Apollo finds Paris in the fighting, points out Achilles and aims the shot. The killing itself is never described: what follows is the pyre, the ash that would not fill a small urn set against a glory that would fill the world, and the shield that sets the survivors quarrelling until the son of Tantalus puts the burden off himself and hands the decision to the assembled Greek leaders.

sentences.t:
At deus, aequoreas qui cuspide temperat undas,
in volucrem corpus nati Phaethontida versum
mente dolet patria saevumque perosus Achillem
exercet memores plus quam civiliter iras,
sentences.l: But the god who with his point controls the waters of the sea grieves in a father's mind for the body of his son, turned into a Phaethontian bird, and, having conceived a hatred of savage Achilles, plies angers that remember, more than citizen-fashion,
sentences.i: But the god who governs the sea's waters with his trident grieves as a father for his son's body, changed into a Phaethontian bird; and in his hatred of savage Achilles he works a grudge that will not forget, further than any citizen may,
sentences.n: Neptune is not named: the periphrasis aequoreas qui cuspide temperat undas “who with his point controls the waters of the sea” identifies him by the weapon. Phaethontida is a Greek accusative singular agreeing with volucrem, “a Phaethontian bird” — the swan; the son himself is not named here. perosus is the perfect participle of perodi and is active in force, “having come to hate”. memores iras “angers that remember” is a poetic plural for one grudge, and plus quam civiliter “more than in citizen fashion” measures it against what a fellow-citizen may decently show: the anger is a despot's.

sentences.t:
iamque fere tracto duo per quinquennia bello
talibus intonsum conpellat Sminthea dictis:
sentences.l: and now, the war having been dragged through nearly two five-year stretches, he accosts the unshorn Sminthian with words of this kind:
sentences.i: and now, with the war dragged out for nearly ten years, he accosts the unshorn Sminthian in words like these:
sentences.n: tracto ... bello is an ablative absolute, “the war having been dragged out”; fere “nearly” qualifies the span duo quinquennia, two stretches of five years. Sminthea is the Greek accusative of Smintheus, a cult title of Apollo in the Troad; intonsum “unshorn” points to the god's uncut hair, the mark of his unaging youth. talibus ... dictis is an ablative of means, framing the speech that follows.

sentences.t:
“O mihi de fratris longe gratissime natis,
inrita qui mecum posuisti moenia Troiae,
ecquid, ubi has iamiam casuras adspicis arces,
ingemis?
sentences.l: “O by far the most welcome to me of my brother's children, you who set up along with me the walls of Troy — walls made void — do you groan at all, when you look at these citadels that are at this very moment about to fall?
sentences.i: “O dearest to me by far of my brother's sons, you who raised Troy's walls together with me, and raised them for nothing — does it draw a groan from you at all, when you look at these towers on the very point of falling?
sentences.n: de fratris ... natis is a partitive with de and the ablative after the superlative gratissime; Neptune's brother is Jupiter, so the addressee is Apollo. inrita “made void” is predicative with moenia: the walls the two gods raised together, as mecum “with me” claims, are proving to have been raised for nothing. ecquid is the interrogative adverb “at all?”, and it governs ingemis across the whole intervening clause ubi ... arces. casuras is the future participle of cado agreeing with arces, and iamiam “now now” means at this very moment.

sentences.t:
Aut ecquid tot defendentia muros
milia caesa doles?
sentences.l: Or do you at all grieve for so many thousands cut down defending the walls?
sentences.n: doles takes a plain accusative object here, tot milia “so many thousands”, where English needs a preposition. defendentia is a present participle, neuter accusative plural agreeing with milia and governing muros, while caesa, the perfect passive participle, agrees with milia too: the thousands are defending and cut down at once. ecquid is repeated from the question before.

sentences.t:
Ecquid, ne persequar omnes,
Hectoris umbra subit circum sua Pergama tracti?
sentences.l: Does — not to go through them all — the shade of Hector, dragged round his own Pergama, come up before you?
sentences.i: Does the ghost of Hector, dragged round his own Pergama — not to run through them all — rise into your mind?
sentences.n: ne persequar omnes is a parenthetical negative purpose clause with the first-person subjunctive, “not to go through them all”: Neptune breaks off his own list. The genitive Hectoris opens the line and its participle tracti closes it, with umbra subit circum sua Pergama standing between them. subit is used absolutely of something rising into the mind. Pergama is the neuter plural name of Troy's citadel.

sentences.t:
cum tamen ille ferox belloque cruentior ipso
vivit adhuc, operis nostri populator, Achilles.
sentences.l: while nevertheless that fierce one, and bloodier than war itself, is alive still — the ravager of our work, Achilles.
sentences.i: and all the while that savage, bloodier than the war itself, is still alive: the wrecker of what we built, Achilles.
sentences.n: cum with the indicative here means “while, whereas”, setting the survival of Achilles against everything Neptune has just listed. belloque ... ipso is an ablative of comparison after cruentior “bloodier”. The name Achilles is held back to the last word of its line, after the apposition operis nostri populator “the ravager of our work” — the work being the walls. ferox and cruentior are Neptune's words for the man, not the poem's verdict on him.

sentences.t:
Det mihi se! faxo, triplici quid cuspide possim,
sentiat;
sentences.l: Let him give himself to me! I will see to it that he feel what I am able to do with my three-pronged point;
sentences.i: Let him only come within my reach! I will make him feel what I can do with the trident's three prongs;
sentences.n: Det ... se is a jussive subjunctive, “let him put himself in my way”. faxo is an old form of the future perfect of facio used as a plain future, “I will see to it”, and it takes the subjunctive sentiat directly, with no ut. quid ... possim is an indirect question serving as the object of sentiat. triplici cuspide is the trident, the same weapon the periphrasis at the opening of the part named simply cuspide.

sentences.t:
at quoniam concurrere comminus hosti
non datur, occulta necopinum perde sagitta!”
sentences.l: but since it is not granted to close with the enemy hand to hand, destroy him unexpecting with a hidden arrow!”
sentences.i: but since I am not allowed to clash with the enemy hand to hand, kill him off his guard with an arrow he never sees!”
sentences.n: non datur “it is not granted” is impersonal, with the infinitive concurrere; hosti is a dative governed by that verb, “to clash with the enemy”. comminus “hand to hand” is the whole difficulty: the sea-god cannot meet Achilles on the field. necopinum “not expecting it” is the accusative object of perde and describes Achilles at the moment of the shot, occulta ... sagitta the ablative of means. Neptune asks for an ambush in plain words, and the poem lets him ask for it plainly.

sentences.t:
Adnuit atque animo pariter patruique suoque
Delius indulgens nebula velatus in agmen
pervenit Iliacum mediaque in caede virorum
rara per ignotos spargentem cernit Achivos
tela Parim fassusque deum “Quid spicula perdis
sanguine plebis?” ait.
sentences.l: He nodded assent, and the Delian, indulging his uncle's mind equally and his own, veiled in cloud, came into the Trojan column, and in the middle of the slaughter of men he sees Paris scattering his occasional shafts among unknown Achaeans, and, having declared the god, says: “Why are you wasting your darts on the blood of the common crowd?”
sentences.i: He nodded, and the Delian, humouring his uncle's mind and his own alike, wrapped in cloud, made his way into the Trojan ranks; and there, in the thick of the killing, he sees Paris spraying the odd arrow among Achaeans nobody knows, and, showing the god he is, says: “Why are you wasting your arrows on the blood of the common crowd?”
sentences.n: Delius “the Delian” is Apollo, named from his birth-island. indulgens takes the dative animo, one mind shared between patrui “his uncle's” and suo “his own”, with pariter “equally” standing in front of the pair. nebula velatus “veiled in cloud” is how a god enters a battlefield unseen. rara ... tela “scattered shafts” and ignotos “unknown” together make Paris's shooting aimless — he is spending arrows on nobodies. fassus is the perfect participle of the deponent fateor and is active, “having declared the god”, that is, having dropped the disguise. Note that adnuit and pervenit are each spelt the same in the present and the perfect, and this edition marks no vowel lengths, so their tense cannot be told from the form; cernit and ait are unambiguously present. The literal reads the two ambiguous verbs as perfects and leaves the other two present, so the alternation the Latin allows stays visible.

sentences.t:
“Siqua est tibi cura tuorum,
vertere in Aeaciden caesosque ulciscere fratres!”
sentences.l: “If there is any care in you for your own people, turn yourself against the descendant of Aeacus and avenge your slaughtered brothers!”
sentences.i: “If you have any care at all for your own, turn on Aeacus' descendant and avenge your murdered brothers!”
sentences.n: Siqua is si with the indefinite qua agreeing with cura, “if any care”; tibi is a dative of the possessor with est. vertere is not the infinitive but the second-person singular imperative of the passive used in the middle sense, “turn yourself”. Aeaciden is a Greek accusative; since Aeacus was the father of Peleus, the patronymic reaches Achilles at one remove, grandson rather than son. caesos ... fratres are Paris's own brothers, and the possessive is left to be supplied from tuorum.

sentences.t:
Dixit et ostendens sternentem Troica ferro
corpora Peliden, arcus obvertit in illum
certaque letifera direxit spicula dextra.
sentences.l: He spoke, and pointing out the son of Peleus laying low Trojan bodies with the sword, he turned the bow against him and aimed the unerring darts with a death-bringing right hand.
sentences.i: He spoke, and showing him Peleus' son strewing the ground with Trojan bodies, sword in hand, he turned the bow that way and laid the shafts that do not miss with a hand that carries death.
sentences.n: The subject of obvertit and direxit is still Apollo, carried on from ostendens: grammatically it is the god who turns the bow and lays the shot, and the archer's own share in it is left unsaid. sternentem ... Peliden is a present participle with the Greek accusative Peliden “Peleus's son”, wrapped round its own object Troica ... corpora, the four words interlaced across the line-end. arcus is fourth-declension and here accusative, the plural form standing for the one bow. certa “unerring” belongs to spicula and letifera “death-bringing” to dextra, each adjective parked well away from its noun.

sentences.t:
Quod Priamus gaudere senex post Hectora posset,
hoc fuit:
sentences.l: What old Priam could rejoice at after Hector — this was it:
sentences.i: This was the one thing old Priam could take joy in after Hector:
sentences.n: quod ... posset is a relative clause of characteristic with the imperfect subjunctive, and the whole clause is the subject of fuit, picked up by hoc “this”. gaudere takes the neuter accusative quod as an internal object, “to rejoice at which”. post Hectora keeps the Greek accusative of the name; the sense is “after Hector's death”.

sentences.t:
ille igitur tantorum victor, Achille,
victus es a timido Graiae raptore maritae!
sentences.l: you then, that conqueror of men so great, Achilles, were conquered by the cowardly carrier-off of a Greek wife!
sentences.i: So you, the conqueror of men so great, Achilles — you were beaten by the coward who carried off a Greek wife!
sentences.n: The poem turns from narrating to addressing the dead man: Achille is a vocative and victus es second person. ille ... victor is nominative, standing in apposition to the “you” of victus es rather than agreeing with the vocative. victor and victus es set one root against itself, active against passive, in the same sentence. timido is contempt for Paris, and it is the poem's own here rather than a character's; raptor is the man who carries a woman off, and Graiae ... maritae “of a Greek wife” names Helen without naming her.

sentences.t:
At si femineo fuerat tibi Marte cadendum,
Thermodontiaca malles cecidisse bipenni!
sentences.l: But if you had had to fall by a womanish Mars, you would have preferred to have fallen by a Thermodontian double-axe!
sentences.i: But if you had to go down in a woman's kind of warfare, you would rather have fallen to a Thermodontian battle-axe!
sentences.n: cadendum ... fuerat tibi is the gerundive of obligation with the dative of the person, “you had to fall”; the pluperfect indicative of the if-clause and the imperfect subjunctive malles carry the unreal sense between them. femineo ... Marte is Mars for warfare by metonymy, hence “a womanish war”. The Thermodontiaca bipennis is the double axe of the Amazons, named from the Thermodon in their country: the reproach is that if a woman's war had to kill him, an Amazon would at least have been the honourable form of it.

sentences.t:
Iam timor ille Phrygum, decus et tutela Pelasgi
nominis, Aeacides, caput insuperabile bello,
arserat:
sentences.l: Now that terror of the Phrygians, the glory and safeguard of the Pelasgian name, the descendant of Aeacus, a head unconquerable in war, had burned:
sentences.i: By now that terror of the Phrygians, the pride and protection of the Pelasgian name, Aeacus' descendant, a head no war could master, had burned:
sentences.n: Four appositions pile up — timor ille Phrygum, decus et tutela Pelasgi nominis, Aeacides, caput insuperabile bello — before the single verb arserat “had burned” arrives to hold them, at the head of its own line. Phrygum “of the Phrygians” means the Trojans and Pelasgi nominis “of the Pelasgian name” the Greeks: he is defined from both sides at once. caput “head” stands for the whole man. arserat is intransitive — he burned, on the pyre.

sentences.l: the same god had armed him and the same was burning him; now he is ash, and of an Achilles so great there remains a something-I-know-not-what, such as would not fill a small urn well:
sentences.i: the same god had armed him, and the same god was burning him; he is ash already, and of an Achilles so great there is left I know not what — a something that would not properly fill even a small urn:
sentences.n: armarat is a syncopated pluperfect for armaverat. deus idem is the god of fire, who made the armour and now consumes the body; the two tenses hold the making apart from the burning, pluperfect against imperfect. Magnus prints cremabat “was burning”; some editions print cremarat, a pluperfect, which flattens that contrast. nescio quid works as a single indefinite noun, “a something, I do not know what”. quod ... conpleat is a relative clause of characteristic, subjunctive: the sort of remnant that would not fill the urn. parvam agrees with urnam across the intervening relative pronoun; some editions print parvum, which makes the remnant small instead of the urn.

sentences.t: at vivit totum quae gloria conpleat orbem!
sentences.l: but there lives a glory such as would fill the whole world!
sentences.n: Another relative clause of characteristic, conpleat again in the subjunctive and deliberately the same verb as the line before: what would not fill a small urn would fill the world. quae gloria has its noun drawn inside the relative clause, a normal Latin arrangement, and totum ... orbem is wrapped around the whole of it.

sentences.t:
Haec illi mensura viro respondet, et hac est
par sibi Pelides nec inania Tartara sentit.
sentences.l: This measure answers to that man, and by this the son of Peleus is equal to himself and does not feel the empty Tartara.
sentences.i: This is the measure that matches the man; taken by this, Peleus' son is his own size, and feels nothing of the empty underworld.
sentences.n: mensura “measure” is the glory of the line before, not the urn: respondet with the dative illi ... viro means it corresponds to, is proportionate to, the man. hac is the ablative of that same mensura. par sibi “equal to himself” says he is still at his own scale — the urn did not shrink him. inania Tartara is a neuter plural for the underworld, inania “empty” both of substance and, for him, of any hold.

sentences.t:
Ipse etiam, ut, cuius fuerit, cognoscere posses
bella movet clipeus, deque armis arma feruntur.
sentences.l: The shield itself too, so that you might learn whose it had been, sets wars going, and over arms arms are taken up.
sentences.i: Even the shield itself starts a war — so that one could tell whose it had been — and weapons are wielded over weapons.
sentences.n: Ipse stands at the head of the sentence and its noun clipeus does not arrive until the next line, with the purpose clause ut ... cognoscere posses between them. posses is a second-person imperfect subjunctive of the indefinite “you”, anyone at all, not the Achilles addressed above. cuius fuerit is an indirect question with the perfect subjunctive, “whose it had been”. deque armis arma feruntur turns the noun back on itself: arma are the prize and arma the means.

sentences.t:
Non ea Tydides, non audet Oileos Aiax,
non minor Atrides, non bello maior et aevo
poscere, non alii:
sentences.l: Those things Tydeus' son does not dare to ask for, nor does Oileus's Ajax dare, nor the lesser son of Atreus, nor the one greater in war and in age, nor the rest:
sentences.i: Tydeus' son does not dare ask for them, nor Ajax son of Oileus, nor the lesser son of Atreus, nor the one greater in war and in years — nor anyone else:
sentences.n: ea is neuter accusative plural, the arms, the object of poscere; the one verb audet governs the whole list, and poscere is held back to the third line of it, so the English has to say “dare” twice where the Latin says it once. non is repeated five times across the three lines. Tydides is Diomedes; Oileos is a Greek genitive, so this Aiax is the son of Oileus, not the Telamonian of the next clause; minor Atrides is Menelaus and bello maior et aevo Agamemnon, the two sons of Atreus told apart by war and by age.

sentences.t:
solis Telamone creato
Laerteque fuit tantae fiducia laudis.
sentences.l: to those alone begotten of Telamon and of Laertes there was the confidence for a distinction so great.
sentences.i: Only the son of Telamon and the son of Laertes had the confidence to claim a distinction so great.
sentences.n: fuit with the dative is the ordinary Latin way of saying that someone had something: the fiducia “confidence” belongs to the two men, and tantae ... laudis is a genitive after it, confidence for so great a distinction. As Magnus prints the line, solis is dative plural while creato is dative singular, so the two do not agree in number, and Telamone and Laerte stand as ablatives of origin; the sense the passage requires is plainly “to these two alone”, and the literal reaches it by taking the single creato with both fathers at once. Some editions print creatis ... Laerta, a dative plural with the two ablatives, which removes the difficulty. Telamon's son is Ajax, and Laertes's son is named here only through his father.

sentences.t:
A se Tantalides onus invidiamque removit
Argolicosque duces mediis considere castris
iussit et arbitrium litis traiecit in omnes.
sentences.l: From himself the descendant of Tantalus removed the burden and the ill-will, and ordered the Argive leaders to take their seats in the middle of the camp, and threw the arbitration of the suit across onto them all.
sentences.i: The descendant of Tantalus got the burden and the ill-feeling off himself: he ordered the Argive leaders to sit down in the middle of the camp, and passed the judgement of the quarrel across to all of them.
sentences.n: Tantalides “descendant of Tantalus” is Agamemnon, named by his line rather than by his name, as Aeacides and Pelides have been. onus invidiamque is a pair — the weight of the decision and the resentment it would earn. mediis ... castris is an ablative of place with no preposition, normal in verse, and considere is an infinitive after iussit with the accusative Argolicos duces. arbitrium litis is the language of the courts, the arbitration of a suit, and traiecit in omnes “threw it across onto them all” makes the whole gathering the judge.
